titre: The Amen Break: Seven Seconds Without Royalties
accroche: A seven-second drum roll, recorded in 1969 for a B-side, becomes the rhythmic foundation of thousands of tracks without royalties
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1969, the soul group The Winstons record “Color Him Father,” a single that reaches number seven on the Billboard Hot 100 and number two on the rhythm and blues chart. Its composer, Richard Spencer, receives for it in 1970 the Grammy for Best Rhythm & Blues Song. The B-side, “Amen, Brother,” recorded in early 1969 in Atlanta, is an instrumental drawn from a gospel song. The single is released in May 1969 on Metromedia and, overshadowed by the success of the A-side, this B-side goes almost unnoticed. About one minute twenty-six seconds in, drummer Gregory Coleman plays a drum roll alone, for seven seconds.

## From a DJ compilation to thousands of tracks

In 1986, this handful of seconds lands on a compilation made for disc jockeys, *Ultimate Breaks and Beats*, designed to give turntables rhythmic loops to mix. Electronic samplers, which make it possible to extract a fragment of sound and loop it at will, make it an ideal material: Salt-N-Pepa sample it as early as 1986, then Mantronix and N.W.A in 1988. In the early 1990s, the “Amen break” becomes a pillar of British jungle and drum'n'bass. Wikipedia today counts it in thousands of tracks across widely varying genres.

## A deadline that ran out without his knowing

Richard Spencer, who led The Winstons, had composed “Color Him Father” and held the copyright to the song. He learns of these reuses only in 1996, when an executive asks him for the original tape. According to Wikipedia, the statute of limitations for an infringement suit was then three years, and he could no longer sue. NME spells out the American rule: one had to sue within thirty-six months of the sampling. Neither he nor Gregory Coleman, the drummer who played the break, ever received royalties for this break. Coleman dies homeless and destitute in 2006; Spencer will say he thinks it unlikely that Coleman ever grasped the effect of those seven seconds on music.

In 2015, British DJs Martyn Webster and Steve Theobald launch an online fundraiser for Richard Spencer. In November he receives a check for 24,000 pounds sterling, according to NME and Mixmag. This is not the payment of a right, but a gift from fans and DJs. Spencer, who had at first called these uses plagiarism, will later say he finds them flattering. The three-year clock was running while the break circulated, and its author knew nothing of it.

citation.texte: It's not the worst thing that can happen to you.
citation.source: Ellen Otzen, “Six seconds that shaped 1,500 songs,” BBC News, 2015, quoted in Wikipedia, “Richard Lewis Spencer”

carte.punch: Seven seconds of 1969 drumming, in thousands of tracks, with no royalties for their creators
carte.idee: In 1969, drummer Gregory Coleman records a seven-second drum roll for the B-side of a soul single. Looped by samplers starting in 1986, it ends up in thousands of tracks, with no royalties for their creators. Richard Spencer, the rights holder, only learned of it in 1996.

quiz.question: Why was Richard Spencer unable to claim royalties on the Amen break?
choix: He only learned of the reuse in 1996, after the three-year American statute of limitations had run out
Gregory Coleman, who created the break, alone held the rights to the recording
He had authorized DJs to sample the break as early as the 1980s
The 1969 B-side had never been commercially released, only recorded in the studio
quiz.explication: Spencer, owner of the song's rights, only learns of the reuse in 1996, when the statute of limitations for an infringement suit (three years under American law, according to Wikipedia and NME) had passed. The other answers are contradicted by the sources: Coleman did not hold the rights, the B-side was released commercially with the single, and Spencer, who called these uses plagiarism, authorized nothing.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which group released “Amen, Brother” as a B-side, and in what year?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Winstons record “Amen, Brother” as the B-side of “Color Him Father,” a single released on Metromedia in May 1969.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who plays the seven-second drum roll that would become the Amen break?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is drummer Gregory Coleman who plays this roll alone, about one minute twenty-six seconds into the track, according to the entry.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What allowed the Amen break to spread into thousands of tracks starting in 1986?
choix: Its purchase by a record company that licensed it for free
Its release into the public domain upon its 1969 release
Its inclusion on a compilation made for DJs, looped using samplers
Its mandatory use imposed by a music-industry standard
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1986 compilation Ultimate Breaks and Beats makes this fragment available to DJs, and electronic samplers make it possible to extract it and loop it at will.
